summaries.example: Think about two red apples. Each apple is a different thing, but both have the property of being red. Philosophers ask whether “redness” is something real that both apples share, or whether we only use the word “red” because the apples look alike. They also ask whether a property can belong to many things at once.
summaries.summary: A property is a feature that can be said of something, such as being green, heavy, or a leaf. The entry examines whether properties are real parts of the world and how they connect objects with facts and statements. A major question is whether one shared universal explains why many different things are alike. Realists accept such universals; nominalists and conceptualists offer alternatives involving language or mind-dependent concepts. The entry also discusses individual property-instances called tropes, relations, kinds of properties, and the ways properties help explain science and language.
key_ideas: We talk about properties when we say what things are like or what they have.
A universal can be shared by many different things, while a particular is one individual thing.
Some philosophers think properties are real and mind-independent. Others explain similarities without universals.
Properties may include relations, such as being taller than or loving someone.
Philosophers also ask how properties fit into facts, science, language, and laws of nature.
summaries.why_it_matters: Properties help us describe and compare the world. They may explain why different objects can belong to the same group, why science talks about mass and temperature, and how sentences such as “the apple is red” can be true. Thinking about properties also teaches us that simple words can hide deep questions about what exists.

important_terms.definition: A feature or way something is, such as being red, round, heavy, or honest.
A single thing, such as one apple or one chair, rather than a feature shared by many things.
A property that can be shared by different things, such as being red or weighing 300 grams.
A view that properties are real features that do not depend only on our minds or words.
A view that rejects mind-independent universals, sometimes explaining similarities using words, ideas, or individual property-instances.
The connection between a thing and a property it has; for example, an apple and its redness.

questions_to_think_about: If two objects look alike, must they share one property?
Is “being red” something in the world, an idea in our minds, or only a word?
Can a property belong to another property?
Are relationships, such as “next to,” properties too?

summaries.example: Suppose two gases have the same temperature. One view says each gas instantiates a universal property, temperature-at-a-certain-value, which can occur in different samples. Another view might treat each sample as having its own particularized temperature-instance, or trope, and explain the similarity between them through resemblance. Scientific theory may then raise a further question: is temperature identical with mean molecular kinetic energy, or are these distinct properties connected by a scientific reduction?
summaries.summary: The entry studies properties as predicable and exemplifiable features of things. It focuses on properties understood as universals, while comparing them with particulars and tropes. Universals are invoked to explain objective resemblance, classification, general language, and scientific generalizations, but their existence and identity conditions remain disputed. Realism treats them as mind-independent; nominalism rejects them, often appealing to predicates or tropes; conceptualism appeals to mind-dependent concepts. The discussion extends to relations, propositions and states of affairs, simple and complex properties, structural properties, and the sparse-versus-abundant debate. It also considers whether scientific properties are essentially categorical or dispositional, and how formal property theories support semantics and mathematics.
key_ideas: Predicates are linguistic expressions, while properties are the entities or features that predicates may express; their extensions and meanings need not coincide.
The one-over-many problem motivates universals: one property seems to explain why numerically different things resemble one another and fall under one general term.
Realists disagree about whether universals exist independently of instances or only in instantiated things. Nominalists and conceptualists reject mind-independent universals in different ways.
Tropes replace shared universals with particularized property-instances and typically require resemblance classes to explain objective similarities.
Relations can be properties attributed to several objects, but asymmetric relations raise questions about order: loving someone is not the same state as being loved by that person.
Properties are important in propositions, states of affairs, scientific laws, quantities, natural kinds, formal semantics, and theories of mathematics.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory of properties connects an ordinary grammatical fact—saying that something is F—with major questions in metaphysics. It affects how we understand resemblance, classification, causation, laws of nature, scientific reduction, mental content, and mathematical foundations. The competing views show that explaining how language and science work may require different kinds of ontological commitment, and that no single account is treated as settled in the entry.

important_terms.definition: An entity that can be attributed to an object or other entity and can be instantiated by it; examples include being red and having a certain mass.
A property capable of being instantiated by more than one particular, apparently allowing one feature to be shared across different locations.
An individual entity that is not itself a shareable universal, such as a particular object or, on trope theories, a particularized property-instance.
The relation or linkage by which an object, property, or other item has a property.
A particularized property-instance, usually dependent on one object, proposed as an alternative to a shareable universal.
A view holding that universals exist independently of human thought or language.
A view denying mind-independent universals; versions may appeal to predicates, tropes, or other resources.
A property understood through the powers or effects it can produce in suitable conditions, such as fragility.

questions_to_think_about: Does using a general predicate commit us to a corresponding property?
Could two properties have exactly the same instances yet differ in meaning?
Would a trope theory explain similarity as well as a theory of universals?
Are scientific properties fundamentally categorical features, dispositions, or both?
Why might a theory of properties need to restrict self-predication?

summaries.example: Imagine three students carrying backpacks that each weigh 5 kilograms. The word “heavy” describes a feature, but philosophers can ask what makes the students similar. A realist might say they all share a universal property, weighing 5 kilograms. A nominalist might say there is no shared feature apart from the students and the way we group or describe them. A trope theorist might say each student has a different weight-instance, with the instances resembling one another.
summaries.summary: Properties are features or ways things are, including colors, shapes, weights, abilities, and relations. The central issue is whether properties are real entities and, especially, whether universals can be shared by many different objects. This shared feature seems to explain why objects resemble one another and why general words apply to them. Realists accept universals, with some treating them as independent of instances and others locating them in things. Nominalists reject mind-independent universals, while conceptualists appeal to concepts. The entry also compares universals with tropes, examines how properties enter propositions and facts, and considers their roles in science, language, and logic.
key_ideas: Properties are not the same as predicates: predicates are parts of language, while properties are what predicates may mean or express.
The one-over-many problem asks how many different objects can be alike in one respect, such as color, shape, or weight.
Realists accept universals, but they disagree about whether universals exist independently of their examples or only when things instantiate them.
Nominalists deny mind-independent universals, while conceptualists replace them with concepts that depend on minds.
A relation, such as loving or being between, may count as a property because it is attributed to several objects together.
Philosophers debate whether properties are sparse and scientifically important or abundant enough to match every meaningful way of describing things.
summaries.why_it_matters: Our ability to classify things, make general statements, and formulate scientific laws seems to depend on features that can apply in more than one case. The debate over properties asks whether those features are genuinely part of reality or are supplied by language or thought. It also influences how we understand relations, causes, laws, meanings, and the difference between an object’s actual features and the ways it could have been.

important_terms.definition: A feature that can be attributed to something, such as a color, shape, weight, or ability.
One individual thing, not a feature that can be shared by many different things.
A repeatable property that different objects can have, such as being circular or weighing 5 kilograms.
The idea that an object has a property; a red apple exemplifies redness.
An individual property-instance tied to one object, used by some philosophers instead of universals.
The view that universals exist independently of people’s minds and language.
The view that there are no mind-independent universals; it may explain grouping through language, tropes, or resemblance.
A feature understood as a capacity to produce effects in certain circumstances, such as being fragile.

questions_to_think_about: When two objects are similar, what exactly explains their similarity?
Could two properties have the same examples but different meanings?
Does a relationship like “older than” belong to one object, or to a pair of objects?
Should an unobserved or uninstantiated property count as real?
Are properties powers to act, ordinary qualities, or both?
